articles.headline: Hackers breached an unclassified CIA and ODNI system used for open-source intelligence
articles.summary: The New York Times reported that an unclassified CIA and ODNI network holding open-source intelligence was breached. A source says no classified data was involved and the issue is resolved; who did it, and what was taken, is unknown.
impacts: Even unclassified intelligence systems hold analysis workflows that adversaries can learn from.
Data from other government agencies may also have been exposed, though the scope is unclear.
It lands in a week of US outages and breaches, so officials are being pressed on whether they are linked.
details: On November 24, The New York Times reported that hackers breached an unclassified computer system used by the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. The Associated Press, citing one person familiar with the incident who spoke anonymously, confirmed that an unclassified CIA system was breached.

The affected system is used to analyze open-source intelligence, meaning material gathered from public sources. That source told the AP the breach did not involve classified information and that the issue has been resolved. Bloomberg, as summarized by Investing.com, also cited one person saying the system does not handle classified information and the technical problem is fixed.

An ODNI representative said there have been no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems. The CIA declined to comment, according to Bloomberg. The Times said data belonging to other government agencies was also believed to have been exposed, but the scope is unclear, and investigators have not said who was responsible.

Fox News, citing sources, reported that the breach happened last week on the same day the FBI was hit, and that the CIA, ODNI and FBI were all breached that day. Two Pentagon officials told Fox the Department of War was not breached. Fox's page also describes the FBI breach as more serious because it affected the National Crime Information Center; that detail comes from the page's sidebar, and the AP described it only as an apparent hack of a national law enforcement database.

The AP noted that the NSA's internal network was offline for a time last week. The administration says the outages are not a coordinated cyberattack, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton attributed them largely to rushed patching and upgrades.

What is unknown matters most: no one has said how the attackers got in, what they took, or whether the CIA, ODNI and FBI incidents are connected. All of the claims about the data being unclassified and the matter being resolved come from anonymous sources and one agency statement, not from an independent review.

articles.headline: Oregon and Virginia sue Musk's companies, saying Grok's weak safeguards were 'a feature'
articles.summary: Two state attorneys general sued SpaceX, X Corp and SpaceXSI over sexualized images made with Grok, including child sexual abuse material. The companies say they tightened protections and blame users who broke the rules. No court has ruled.
impacts: Launching image tools without standard safeguards may now carry state-level legal risk.
The suits test whether 'consumer protection' law can reach AI image generators.
People can be depicted in sexual images they never consented to, and fixes arrive after the harm.
details: On Monday, November 23, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones, both Democrats, filed separate but similar consumer-protection suits. Virginia's was filed in a Richmond state court. The defendants include SpaceX, X Corp and SpaceXSI, SpaceX's AI unit.

The core allegation is that the companies skipped industry-standard safeguards when launching Grok's image tools, leading to widespread child sexual abuse material and nonconsensual intimate imagery. Virginia alleges Grok's published instructions told it to 'assume good intent' and set minimal limits on sexual content, and that X made false, deceptive or misleading statements in January about image-editing fixes.

According to the reports, image generation and editing rolled out to all users in December 2025. By January there was a global backlash, Malaysia and Indonesia announced temporary bans, and Grok then limited image tools for non-paying users. Virginia's suit says that change 'simply made that generation profitable.' The suit also alleges users could still make such images through a standalone app and website, and that jailbreaks were not fixed promptly. In January, 35 attorneys general had urged the company to block such material.

The states seek injunctions and the giving up of 'ill-gotten gains'; Virginia also seeks $2,500 per willful violation, with the total to be proven at trial. Jones said, 'For these Defendants, weak safeguards were not a failure but a feature.' Rayfield called it 'an intentional business decision that they purposely profited off of.'

The companies dispute the framing. X's Safety account called such content 'abhorrent', blamed users who broke the terms, and said protections were tightened this year. SpaceXSI says it acts against abusers and has filed at least three federal suits against users.
These are allegations in complaints, not findings. What to watch is whether other states join, and whether a court accepts that skipping safeguards is itself a deceptive practice.

articles.headline: A suspected Russian warship jammed GPS for more than 100 flights over the North Sea
articles.summary: Pilots over the North Sea and UK airspace lost GPS on November 9, with some losing signal for about 20 minutes. Press and analysts suspect a Russian warship escorting cargo ships; the UK government declined to comment.
impacts: Civil aircraft still depend on GPS for parts of navigation, so jamming far from conflict zones raises routine-flight risk.
Jamming that reaches mobile networks and radio near the coast could affect more than aviation.
Experts see it as a step up in Russia's 'shadow war' against Western countries.
details: According to reporting by Yahoo News UK and UNITED24 Media, GPS interference hit airliners over the North Sea and UK airspace on November 9, and a Russian warship is suspected. That attribution comes from the press and analysts, not from an official finding.

The numbers differ by outlet. The lead says more than 100 passenger flights; about 140 flights across Northern Europe and the North Sea are credited to the iPaper, and about 40 aircraft were in or near UK airspace at the time. Some pilots reportedly lost GPS for around 20 minutes. Flights named by The Mirror include a Ryanair Edinburgh–Rome service, a British Airways London–Stockholm flight and an easyJet Manchester–Egypt flight; those details are not tied to an official source.

The vessel is not named. It was reportedly escorting cargo ships called Lady R, Lady D and Maia-1, linked to military cargo, with NATO vessels reportedly shadowing the convoy. UNITED24, relaying The Sun, says analysts traced the source to about 190 miles off the British coast. The UK government said it was 'unable to comment', and no Russian statement was cited.

Dr Thomas Withington, an electronic warfare specialist, said confirmed Russian involvement would be 'an intensification of the disruption that we've seen so far,' that it was the first time he knew of such jamming this far west, and that he does not expect it to be the last. Former naval intelligence officer James Droxford suggested it could be a reaction to Western surveillance of the ships, given its short duration and location. Ramsey Faragher of the Royal Institute of Navigation said the strength of the interference suggested a military vessel and that closer to the coast mobile networks and DAB radio could also be affected.
UNITED24 also summarizes earlier reports that in May 2026 a British military aircraft carrying the Defence Secretary lost GPS on a flight from Estonia to the UK; those are secondhand summaries.

Aircraft have backup navigation, and nothing in the reporting says any flight was endangered beyond the loss of signal. The open question is attribution: until a government confirms the source, this remains a strong suspicion rather than a finding.

articles.headline: Citizen Lab: 'AdFection' spyware can be delivered through targeted ads with no click
articles.summary: Citizen Lab says an Israeli firm, Discover-Tech, used ad auctions to deliver mercenary spyware code to chosen devices. Whether government and media targets were actually infected is unknown; Al Jazeera devices were targeted.
impacts: Merely loading a web page or app with an ad could be enough for infection in this chain.
Ad-tech lets an attacker pick a victim by advertising ID, browser ID or IP address.
Ad exchanges had listed the vendor for years, so vetting failed before it was removed.
details: Citizen Lab's Report 195, timed with a Confiant investigation, calls AdFection the first public technical confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through targeted ads. An ad renders, requests JavaScript from a Discover-Tech server, and gets code back only if the user is judged eligible; otherwise the server returns nothing. Citizen Lab says the ad display alone can be enough for infection.

Discover-Tech is an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate ad firm. Citizen Lab describes it as a facilitator for several mercenary spyware partners. Its 'Controlium' platform lets customers choose targets by mobile advertising ID, browser ID or IP address, and it appeared on Google and IAB Europe vendor lists from 2020 to 2026.

The scale described is large. Over about 4 billion bid records from March to June 2026, ads with attacker script tags appeared in 75,373 apps and 120,768 websites across 161 countries; at least 718.7 million bids carried script tags. Recorded spend was only about $109,091. An impression does not confirm infection, and Citizen Lab stresses that.

At least 45 Al Jazeera devices were targeted in 2024 and 2025, and Citizen Lab links those attacks to Candiru (since rebranded Integrity Labs) with high confidence, based on a sample whose command servers match a fingerprint it developed. Discover-Tech ads were also shown on networks of NATO, UN and EU bodies, ministries and defense firms. One decrypted link pointed to an IP registered to the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which Citizen Lab presents as an assessment, not proof of who the customer was.

Google ended Discover-Tech's ad exchange access and removed it from its vendor registry in early October, and IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle and Eskimi acted too. Citizen Lab asks regulators to investigate Discover-Tech and Candiru.

Unknown: how many people were really infected, and who the end customers were. Ad-blocking and strict browser settings reduce exposure, but the report is about the ad supply chain, not something an individual can easily audit.

articles.headline: MIT's Esvelt argues vaccines cannot protect us from an engineered pandemic
articles.summary: In an UnHerd essay, biologist Kevin Esvelt says a designed pathogen could evade immunity, citing AI-designed phage genomes and weak DNA-synthesis screening. It is an argument, not a new incident; some of his inferences are unconfirmed.
impacts: Defenses built around a 100-day vaccine timeline may be too slow for a deliberately designed pathogen.
Gene synthesis firms mostly lack effective screening, and no country legally requires it.
AI that designs genomes lowers the skill needed to explore dangerous variants.
details: Kevin Esvelt, who leads the Sculpting Evolution group at the MIT Media Lab, argues in an October 2026 UnHerd essay that natural evolution is 'blind', so vaccines can keep up with it, while an intelligent attacker could design around immunity.

He points to the Soviet bioweapons program, which included a weaponized smallpox strain. A 1971 smallpox outbreak at Aralsk was later linked to an aerosolized test on an Aral Sea island, and the USSR signed the Biological Weapons Convention in 1972 but kept the program running. He also describes hospitals reportedly quarantined in Irkutsk after a plague researcher died, which authorities called 'pneumonia of unknown etiology'. Esvelt infers an engineered agent; that is his inference, not a confirmed fact.

On timelines, countries aim to approve vaccines within 100 days of spotting a novel disease and the US hopes to manufacture enough doses within 130 days. He says that is too slow against a fast or lethal pathogen.

On AI, he cites a 2026 Science study by Stanford and Arc Institute researchers who used Evo genome language models to design bacteriophage genomes, using a phage called ΦX174 as a template. About 300 designs were made and 16 were viable phages that infect E. coli. The authors say the work raises biosafety and biosecurity concerns and that groups doing whole-genome design should consult safety professionals throughout. A companion Perspective said the question is no longer whether generative viral genome design will exist. The same work has a benign side: phage cocktails beat E. coli strains resistant to ΦX174.

Esvelt says his lab showed that all DNA pieces needed to recreate the 1918 flu virus could be legally purchased, that most gene synthesis firms lack effective screening, and that no nation legally requires it. His proposals include stockpiled protective equipment, far-UV light and glycol vapors to neutralize airborne pathogens, germicidal systems in buildings, and screening laws that account for AI-assisted acquisition.
Keep the scale in mind: the phage work involved a bacterial virus, not a human one, and Esvelt's warning about human viruses is a projection.

articles.headline: JAMA Psychiatry: Vanderbilt found 28 'AI psychosis' patients, mostly first episodes
articles.summary: Vanderbilt researchers searched 578,058 clinic notes and found 28 patients whose psychosis involved chatbots, usually amplifying delusions already forming. The condition looks rare, and the study cannot say whether AI causes psychosis.
impacts: Clinicians may need to ask patients about chatbot use, as the lead author urges.
A tool that is always available and agreeable can reinforce a fragile belief.
The numbers are likely an undercount because chatbot use is only noted when a clinician thinks to record it.
details: A JAMA Psychiatry study from Vanderbilt University Medical Center, led by Zachary Bergson and Julia Sheffield, searched 578,058 progress notes from 215,712 behavioral-health patients between December 2022 and April 2026. Two raters reviewed the hits, leaving 187 encounters across 73 patients, sorted into neutral chatbot use (17), AI-related psychotic content without chatbot use (28) and 'AI psychosis' (28).

The 28 AI-psychosis patients are about 0.013% of the center's mental-health patients. Median age was 27.5, 60.7% were in a first psychotic episode (versus 17.6% in the neutral group) and 67.9% were male. ChatGPT was named in 53.6% of records, and 85.7% of interactions came after May 2024, when GPT-4o was released.

The authors classified the chatbot's role as amplifier (64.3%), object (21.4%) or catalyst (10.7%); none were 'coauthor'. Three cases described chatbot use preceding new symptoms. The study notes OpenAI's estimate that about 0.07% of weekly ChatGPT users show possible signs of psychosis or mania, though the populations differ.

The limits are large: one Tennessee center, an observational design, reliance on clinicians documenting chatbot use, an unvalidated four-type scheme, and a GPT-4o timing pattern that could just reflect growing use. Sheffield said, 'We cannot say from this study if AI use causes psychosis or simply exacerbates it.' She called a constantly available harmful technology 'highly concerning' and said it 'requires regulation'.

Iris Sommer of Groningen, who was not involved, urged care with the term 'AI psychosis', saying newer language models seem less likely to validate unlikely beliefs and may help people with no access to care.
Takeaway: real cases exist and cluster among people in a first episode, but the evidence does not show a population-level risk.

articles.headline: Exeter and BAS authors say parts of two ice sheets and a key ocean current may be past tipping points
articles.summary: A report announced November 19 says parts of West Antarctica, Greenland and the Subpolar Gyre may already have crossed tipping points. I could reach only a secondary write-up, which does not say whether the report is peer-reviewed.
impacts: Once a threshold is crossed, ice loss continues even if warming stops, over centuries to millennia.
West Antarctica and Greenland hold enough ice for about 5 m and 7 m of sea-level rise respectively.
A Subpolar Gyre collapse could bring colder, stormier winters to northwest Europe.
details: A report from University of Exeter and British Antarctic Survey authors, announced on November 19, 2026 and building on the 2025 Global Tipping Points Report, says tipping points may already have been crossed in parts of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet (the Amundsen Sea basin, which includes Thwaites and Pine Island glaciers, and possibly the Ronne basin), parts of the Greenland Ice Sheet and the Subpolar Gyre, an ocean current that strongly affects northwest European weather.

The wording is hedged: 'may have crossed'. The secondary article I could open does not give the report's title, the thresholds in question or the authors' confidence, and it does not say whether the report is peer-reviewed. I did not reach an Exeter or BAS primary page, so treat the details below as the article's account.

Full loss of West Antarctica would raise sea level by about 5 m (16 ft) and Greenland by about 7 m (23 ft), with more than 2 billion coastal people at long-term risk. Permafrost, wetland, freshwater and wildfire emissions could amplify warming by 20–30%. A Subpolar Gyre collapse could signal a wider collapse of the AMOC circulation. Small island states could face national-scale displacement. The ice loss itself unfolds over centuries to millennia, but once a threshold is crossed the process continues even if warming stops.

Helen Millman of Exeter said, 'Every fraction of a degree changes how fast and how far the losses go.' Professor Michael Meredith of BAS said, 'Once these icy regions pass their tipping points, there's no rewind button,' and added, 'The science is stark, but it isn't hopeless.'

The recommendations: limit time above 1.5°C, cut methane quickly, scale carbon removal, avoid risky geoengineering (no international governance exists), plan coastal defenses for multi-metre sea-level rise beyond 2100 and fund loss and damage.
Watch for the primary report and any independent response from ice-sheet scientists, who often disagree about exactly where thresholds sit.

articles.headline: ESA report: casualty risk from uncontrolled rocket-stage reentries is above 4% a year
articles.summary: ESA's 2026 Space Environment Report adds a new metric estimating casualty risk from reentering rocket upper stages at over 4% in 2024, double 2020. ESA says risk remains low compared with everyday risks; a researcher projects higher odds over a decade.
impacts: About 124 rocket stages reentered uncontrolled in 2024, more than two a week.
Risk lands on people under flight paths, mostly outside the countries that launch.
Controlled ocean reentry is possible, but is not required of all rockets.
details: ESA's 2026 Space Environment Report introduces a metric for on-ground casualty risk from reentries. As reported by Space.com on September 30, it puts the casualty risk from reentering rocket upper stages at over 4% in 2024, double the 2020 level, and up to 1% for satellite reentries. About 124 rocket stages reentered uncontrolled in 2024. ESA's report says the chance of a casualty 'increased in recent years due to increased traffic.'

These are the report's estimates for 2024. ESA's own page says the casualty probability remains low compared with everyday risks. The 4% figure is an annual risk of at least one casualty somewhere, not a risk to any individual.

Ewan Wright of the University of British Columbia says that if about 124 uncontrolled stage reentries a year continue for a decade, the chance someone is killed by rocket debris is 33%. That is one academic's projection, not an ESA statement. He says, 'All rockets should be required to do controlled reentries into the ocean.'

The ESA page adds context on traffic: in 2025, more than 300 launches put over 4,000 new payloads in orbit, about ten a day, and more than three intact satellites or rocket bodies reenter per day on average. It says controlled rocket-body reentries outnumbered uncontrolled ones for the second year.

Incidents cited include debris in Canton, North Carolina, confirmed as part of a SpaceX Dragon that reentered in May 2024, and metallic spheres on Forrest Beach, Queensland in July 2026, which the Australian Space Agency described as consistent with debris from a foreign rocket body.

Stijn Lemmens, ESA's head of the Space Debris Office, says projections are 'based on extrapolating how we behave now instead of what would be desirable.' Even with zero launches the debris population would keep growing, because fragmentation outpaces natural reentry.

articles.headline: Lab-grown 'mini brains' of about 10,000 neurons decoded braille, and three beat one
articles.summary: University of Bristol researchers fed braille touch data into tiny human-forebrain organoids on electrode arrays. A classifier read the right letter about 61% of the time from one organoid and 83% from three. 'Reading' here means decodable responses.
impacts: Living neural tissue can be used as a physical computing layer for sensor data.
Combining several organoids improved accuracy, though the authors cannot yet say why.
It is an early lab result on one task, far from any practical biocomputer.
details: In a paper in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, University of Bristol researchers led by PhD candidate Tianyi Liu and Dr Benjamin Ward-Cherrier report encoding tactile stimuli for braille recognition with organoids. The organoids are modeled on the human forebrain, under 1 mm across, with about 10,000 neurons plus supporting cells, and sit on multielectrode arrays that stimulate and record.

A tactile sensor captured the 26 braille letters, and the data was converted into stimulation patterns. A simple support vector machine classifier then read the organoid responses. A single organoid gave the right letter about 61% of the time; three together reached about 83%. With added noise filtering, decoding the organoid responses held up better than decoding the degraded input signals directly.

Liu said, 'We can take information from a real tactile sensor, turn it into a form that a living neural network can receive.' The hardware point is that the tissue acted as a processing stage between sensor and classifier.

The caveats are important. The study did not test learning or long-term change, it used one task and a fixed encoding scheme, and the authors cannot yet explain why three organoids beat one. 'Reading' is figurative: the responses were decodable by a classifier, not understood by the tissue.

The wider field is active but early. Researchers have long pitched organoid computing as a lower-energy complement to silicon, and that remains a projection rather than a demonstration. Watch for tests of learning and stability over weeks, which would separate a lab curiosity from a usable component.

articles.headline: Okta: a vishing crew that may be ShinyHunters, now 'INCEPTION', phones staff with fake 'legal' pages
articles.summary: Okta tracks a cluster that phones targets and walks them through fake sign-in pages and MFA prompts. It says the group may have been tied to ShinyHunters and may have rebranded as INCEPTION; the group denies the link.
impacts: A convincing phone call can defeat codes and push-approval MFA.
Passkeys and Okta FastPass are not what this kit is built to beat, according to Okta.
Leak sites turn successful calls into extortion within days.
details: Okta Threat Intelligence researchers Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels describe a cluster they call O-UNC-053, tracked since March 2026. They say it 'may have been' affiliated with ShinyHunters and 'may have' rebranded as INCEPTION, which is an assessment. As of November 16, a new INCEPTION leak site listed data stolen from O-UNC-053 targets.

The method is voice phishing. Operators phone targets and talk them into entering credentials on phishing pages, then approving MFA prompts or sharing one-time codes. Okta says the kit intercepts authentication flows and is not built to defeat phishing-resistant methods such as passkeys and Okta FastPass.

Targets span technology, healthcare, biotech, finance, insurance, entertainment, gaming, retail, transportation, hospitality and legal. Domains follow patterns such as legal-<target>, legaldept-<target> and <target>.legal; the 'legal' theme began in October 2026 and domains are often registered on or within a day of a campaign start. Between March and September, targets appeared on the ShinyHunters leak site 1 to 28 days after their phishing domains were registered.

Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 reported 70-plus legal-themed domains since October, behind Cloudflare, sending non-targeted visitors to the real Okta or NetIQ sign-in. ReversingLabs described the same campaign.

The ShinyHunters leak site went offline in late September after the arrest of three alleged members, and Okta saw no O-UNC-053 listings from early September to early November. INCEPTION says: 'We are not ShinyHunters. We were never ShinyHunters. We are INCEPTION.'

Unknown: whether the leaked data is authentic, whether INCEPTION runs the site itself, and the exact ShinyHunters link. Okta's bottom line is that the operators remain active in vishing for account takeover, theft and extortion, whoever runs the site.

articles.headline: A new Iran-aligned spy group runs its malware through IPFS, targeting Cyprus airlines and Saudi hospitals
articles.summary: Check Point describes Volant Manticore, an espionage group active since about late August 2025, whose KuboShell backdoor takes commands via IPFS. Check Point assesses it likely split from MuddyWater; victim counts were not given.
impacts: Using a public file network for command traffic makes malware harder to block by domain.
Targets shifted from Cyprus telecoms and airlines to Saudi healthcare.
Phishing lures used AI-generated personas and fake CVs.
details: Check Point Research calls Volant Manticore a previously undocumented Iran-aligned espionage group, with evidence of activity since late August 2025. First targets were telecoms, airlines and critical infrastructure in Cyprus, then it shifted to Saudi healthcare, which the article links to escalating Saudi–Houthi hostilities.

KuboShell is a Windows backdoor that uses IPFS, a peer-to-peer file system, for command and control through a hard-coded Pinata access token. It uses the first network adapter's MAC address as the victim ID and registers by uploading a file containing 'hi'. Every 60 seconds it checks Pinata for a command file named after that MAC address, runs it in hidden PowerShell, and returns output only if the command writes it to a results file.
Homa is a follow-on framework that reimplements MuddyWater's MuddyC2Go client in JavaScript. Remote-management tools used include MeshCentral, NetLock and N-able RMM.

Lures varied. A Cyprus airline on Cyprus–Israel routes got phishing with AI-generated personas and fake CVs; a Cypriot defense-related government entity got a macro-enabled document called 'MilitaryHeritageProposal.doc'; and in September 2026 Saudi healthcare got ZIP files named 'AI_Healthcare_Seminar.zip', some sent from a compromised account at a private Saudi hospital.

Check Point 'assesses' that the group likely consists of former MuddyWater operators who split off, and that both are affiliated with Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security. Its reasons are an older MuddyWater framework and playbook, Cyprus targeting that does not fit MuddyWater, and separate infrastructure. The timing of the split, around 2023, is a hypothesis.
Not stated: how many victims there were or which organizations were affected, so the scale of damage is unknown.

articles.headline: Project Zero: flipping one bit in a .NET file let code slip past Windows code-integrity checks
articles.summary: Google's James Forshaw showed that .NET Framework 4's fallback loading could bypass Windows code integrity and VirtualBox process protection. It needs local access, and fixes shipped in September and October, though one route may remain.
impacts: Local attackers could run untrusted code where only signed code should run.
Protected-process protections are only as strong as every loader behind them.
It is not a remote attack; it needs local access and a program willing to load the assembly.
details: Google Project Zero's James Forshaw published a write-up showing that how .NET Framework 4 loads files lets a local attacker run untrusted code past two protections: Windows User Mode Code Integrity (UMCI) and Oracle VirtualBox process hardening.

The mechanism is a fallback. When the normal image load fails, .NET runs the file from a plain memory copy, skipping the image checks. Clearing the IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE bit in a .NET file's header made the image-mapping call reject it, but .NET still ran it. Forshaw wrote, 'This single bit change is all you need to load an untrusted .NET assembly.'

For VirtualBox, any .NET file compiled as AnyCPU triggers the same fallback; he combined that with COM hijacking, where a COM object registered in the current user's settings gets loaded by a protected VirtualBox process. CVE-2026-87268 (VirtualBox 7.2.16 on Windows hosts, CVSS 7.8) was fixed by Oracle in September; it is code execution inside the protected process, not a VM escape.
CVE-2026-108398 covers the .NET Framework 4 UMCI bypass (CVSS 8.8, tested on Windows 11 S Mode). Microsoft fixed it on October 13 and lists it as publicly disclosed but not used in attacks.

For Protected Process Light there is no CVE. By hijacking a COM object that WerSecureFault.exe loads, he ran code in a PPL process at the highest protection level without admin rights. The article says the October fix corrects the UMCI policy check but does not change loading for protected processes, and the researcher says the PPL route should still work.

Timeline: he presented the bypass at 44Con in September, having judged it outside Microsoft's servicing criteria; after .NET developers said the behavior was accidental, he reported it in late September and the fix shipped in October's Patch Tuesday.

articles.headline: Florida's dengue is now mostly homegrown: local cases outnumber travel cases for the first time
articles.summary: WUSF reports 669 locally acquired dengue cases in Florida against 476 travel-related ones, the first time local cases lead. Heavy rain in Central Florida this month may add to the problem.
impacts: Dengue is spreading locally in places that rarely saw it, such as Apopka and Pine Hills.
Standing water after rain gives mosquitoes breeding sites within days.
True numbers are likely higher because infected people can be asymptomatic and still infect mosquitoes.
details: WUSF, Central Florida Public Media, reported on November 24 that Florida's locally acquired dengue cases total 669, versus 476 travel-related cases. The piece says this is the first time in state history that local cases outnumber travel cases.

Orange County has 10 locally acquired cases, its most ever, all in the Apopka and Pine Hills areas. Hillsborough County has 455 cases and Pinellas County has 126. The state total rose by 100 just before the rain, though the article does not say over what period. One death has been recorded this year, an 80-year-old Tampa woman.

Dengue does not normally occur in Central Florida, and most state cases have been linked to travelers, for example from Cuba. East Orange County got 12 inches of rain from November 17 to 20, per the National Weather Service, and Apopka got just over 5 inches. Orange County has recorded 6.59 inches in November so far against 0.07 inches last November, and trap counts are 4 to 6 times higher than last year.

Steve Harrison, director of Orange County Mosquito Control, attributes much of the outbreak to this year's El Niño: a very dry early spring and summer let Aedes aegypti mosquitoes bank eggs, which hatched after later rains. He worries about people moving between Apopka and east Orange County spreading the virus.
The advice is practical: tip, toss or cover containers that hold water, since clearing standing water for up to five days is the most effective step.
What is uncertain: the article gives no projected holiday case count, and the rainfall and trap comparisons are county data over a limited window.

articles.headline: CoreWeave's default-insurance cost passed 1,000 bp as Treasury yields fell; one analyst sees worry
articles.summary: An investingLive analysis notes CoreWeave's 5-year credit-default swaps above 1,000 basis points and Oracle's near 300 while Treasury yields eased. The safe-haven link to AI-credit worries is the author's hypothesis, without fund-flow data.
impacts: Insuring $1 million of CoreWeave debt against default would cost about $100,000 a year at that level.
Falling yields could reflect fear, not optimism, if investors are seeking refuge.
The author says the AI buildout is not suddenly collapsing and infrastructure demand remains strong.
details: Justin Low of investingLive wrote on October 26 that the 10-year Treasury yield was just below 5% after retreating the previous week, oil kept rising on Middle East tensions, and the Nasdaq had its first back-to-back weekly decline since July.

He says CoreWeave's 5-year credit-default swaps surged above 1,000 basis points 'earlier this month', with no date given, and Oracle's approached 300 basis points. His arithmetic checks out: at 1,000 bp, insuring $1 million of CoreWeave debt costs about $100,000 a year, and at 300 bp Oracle's costs about $30,000.

His hypothesis, not an established fact, is that investors may be buying Treasuries as a refuge from AI-credit worries, so yields fall even though lower yields would normally help technology valuations. He says there is 'a good chance' falling yields reflect worry rather than optimism.
The piece gives no data sources or links for the CDS levels and no fund-flow data to support the safe-haven claim, so it is the weakest-sourced item here and should be read as commentary.

The author also says the AI boom is not 'suddenly falling apart' and that demand for AI infrastructure 'remains strong'. Earlier coverage on this page noted CoreWeave's bond yield near 15% in October; the CDS angle is the new part.
What to watch: whether CDS levels on AI-linked borrowers keep widening, and whether independent data on Treasury buying confirms or contradicts the refuge story.

articles.headline: Synchron pauses enrollment after its next-generation brain implant's cable underperforms
articles.summary: Synchron paused trials of its second-generation wireless Stentrode after a performance problem with the lead cable. The company says it found no safety issue and the pause is voluntary; it has not given a restart date.
impacts: Brain implants depend on mundane parts like cables, and one weak part can stall a whole trial.
People with paralysis waiting for the device face a delay of unknown length.
Bringing lead manufacturing in-house suggests supply-chain control matters for implants.
details: Synchron, a Brooklyn company, paused enrollment in trials of its second-generation wireless Stentrode, a brain-computer interface delivered through a blood vessel for people with paralysis. WIRED reported it first on November 12, and the Medical Daily piece I opened is dated November 17.

The fault is a 'performance problem' with the lead, the cable carrying signals from the electrode array in the vessel to the implanted electronics. When signal quality drops, the system cannot reliably turn intent into commands. Synchron says it found no safety issue and that the pause was voluntary, not an FDA order.

The company plans to bring lead design and manufacturing in-house and upgrade the system before restarting. It has not said how many people received the second-generation device, how many were affected or when trials restart. Per WIRED, it is cutting New York jobs and building a San Diego team for an entirely new device.
CEO Tom Oxley said shortly before the news that the system has hundreds of components and one delayed part can slow an FDA submission.

Background: the first-generation device, in an earlier study of four ALS patients, had no serious adverse events at one year, and they used it for shopping, banking and texting. The first US implant was in 2022 at Mount Sinai West, and 2026 studies are planned in Toronto and Australia with about 10 people each. Synchron raised $200 million in a Series D in November 2025.
Uncertain: Medical Daily expects the timeline to patients to slip, and no restart date has been announced.

articles.headline: China unveils '15 landmark' brain-computer interface achievements, but the report doesn't say what they are
articles.summary: China announced 15 brain-computer interface achievements at a Beijing conference and released an industry report. The coverage does not itemize them, they are a government-industry showcase, and the report itself lists weak clinical evidence.
impacts: Workplace-safety uses of brain signals are named beside medical ones.
The report counts 1,175 BCI companies worldwide, with Chinese clusters prominent.
Standards China sets now may shape how brain data is handled later.
details: The Associated Press of Pakistan, datelined Beijing on November 24, says China unveiled 15 achievements at the 2026 Brain-Computer Interface Conference in Changping, Beijing, held November 19 to 22. The article does not itemize them. It says only that they cover signal acquisition, implantable devices, medical rehabilitation and industrial applications, spanning invasive and non-invasive interfaces. No company names or quotes are given.

The conference also released the 'Research Report on the Innovative Development of Brain-Computer Interfaces (2026)', compiled by the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology and the Brain Computer Interface Industrial Alliance.

Industry figures given: 1,175 BCI companies worldwide in 2026, with three Chinese clusters holding 390 of them, which the article calls 77.4% of China's total. Those clusters are the Yangtze River Delta, Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei and the Greater Bay Area.

The report claims the field is moving from one-way signal reading to multimodal, 'AI-native' systems, and that research and medical uses are the main revenue sources while non-medical uses are early. Uses named include neurological rehabilitation, cognitive assessment, human-machine interaction and workplace safety.

The report itself lists challenges: insufficient clinical evidence, incomplete payment and talent systems, unverified long-term reliability and unproven practical demand. Many medical BCI products are still in research, trials or approval.

These 'achievements' are a showcase, not peer-reviewed results, and I could not verify any individually. The unsettling angle is the mix of medical and workplace uses, which raises the question of who controls brain-signal data.

articles.headline: Paradromics and Nvidia want a brain implant's speech decoder to run on a wheelchair-mounted computer
articles.summary: Paradromics and Nvidia announced a collaboration to run the Connexus implant's decoding on Nvidia edge hardware, aiming for much lower speech latency. The targets are plans, not demonstrated results.
impacts: Lower latency could make decoded speech feel more like natural conversation.
Always-on decoder fine-tuning raises review and neural-data management questions.
The roadmap is planned; nothing here has been shown working.
details: Paradromics, based in Austin, Texas, and Nvidia announced a technical collaboration on November 23. Named people include Paradromics CEO Matt Angle, chief science officer Vikash Gilja and Nvidia's David Niewolny. The scope is to put Nvidia Holoscan and edge-AI hardware into the Connexus brain-computer interface stack, moving decoding from a lab cart tethered to a computer to a wheelchair-mountable enclosure.

The current Connexus Control Unit uses a Jetson Orin Nano (up to 40 TOPS); the plan is Jetson AGX Thor, listed at up to 2,070 TFLOPS. The article sets these side by side, but TOPS and TFLOPS are different units, so the comparison is not like-for-like.

Latency, current versus target: direct neural-to-speech is more than 50 ms now with a target under 10 ms; the multi-stage pipeline (decoding, language model, voice synthesis) is 150–300 ms or more now with a target under 100 ms.

Also planned: continuous background fine-tuning of the decoder without interrupting use, and standard kits for research partners through Nvidia's APEX Program. The timeline is late 2026 for porting decoders to Holoscan and sending initial kits to speech-focused partners, with motor decoding for prosthetic limbs and avatars in 2027 and pocket-sized units later, with no date.
Connexus is in the Connect-One Early Feasibility Study, described as FDA-approved under an IDE, focused on speech restoration for people with ALS, stroke or spinal-cord injury.

What is confirmed is that the partnership and roadmap exist. Not demonstrated: the latency targets, the wheelchair enclosure and online fine-tuning. The quotes are promotional, and the article flags unresolved issues such as IRB amendments for adaptive decoders and data management for neural data. I read a secondary aggregator page, not the company's own release.

articles.headline: A glucose-powered implant treated diabetes in animals by stimulating the vagus nerve, with no battery
articles.summary: National University of Singapore researchers report an implant that runs on body glucose and pulses the vagus nerve when sugar stays high. In diabetic animals it improved blood sugar; there is no human data.
impacts: A self-powered implant removes batteries and charging from the design.
Nerve stimulation that regrows beta cells in animals is a new angle on diabetes.
Safety and efficacy must be shown before any human trial.
details: National University of Singapore researchers published a Nature paper titled 'A glucose-powered artificial neuroimmune axis for metabolic control.' The device is an experimental bioelectronic implant called NeuroAxis. The write-up I opened is a SANA article dated November 22; Medical Xpress reportedly covered it on November 20, and I did not open the paper.

A tiny biofuel cell turns glucose in tissue fluid into electricity using gold and platinum nanoparticles: gold helps convert glucose to gluconate, and platinum drives the oxygen reaction that completes the cell. There are no external batteries and no wireless charging.

The implant records glucose every 30 minutes. After five consecutive high readings, about 2.5 hours, it sends pulses to the vagus nerve for three minutes. The vagus nerve links the brain to organs including the liver, pancreas and intestines.

Type 1 diabetic animals showed pancreatic beta-cell growth and increased total beta-cell mass. Type 2 diabetic rats had blood glucose near normal within two weeks, with better insulin sensitivity. Both groups had lower inflammatory markers and less fat in the body and liver.
Benefits lasted through the six-week study, including after stimulation stopped and the implant went to standby around week two.

The caveats are large: the work is animal-only, six weeks is short, the biofuel cell's stability and the glucose trigger thresholds still need work, and safety and efficacy must be shown before human trials.

articles.headline: Study: brief AI help made people give up sooner on hard tasks and do worse alone
articles.summary: A randomized preprint with 1,222 participants found AI assistance improved performance while available, but people then did worse without it and were more likely to quit. It is a preprint and tests short lab sessions.
impacts: Frequent instant answers may erode the habit of working through difficulty.
Effects shown are short-term; lasting harm is not established.
The authors say AI should be designed for long-term competence, not only task completion.
details: The paper 'AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance' (arXiv 2604.04721) is by Grace Liu, Brian Christian, Tsvetomira Dumbalska, Michiel A. Bakker and Rachit Dubey. The first version appeared April 6, 2026 and the latest I saw is version 6 from October 13, 2026, so the date here is the latest revision.
The design is a set of randomized controlled trials with 1,222 participants in total, on mathematical reasoning and reading comprehension tasks.
The finding is that AI assistance improves performance while it is available. Afterward, people perform worse without it and are more likely to give up.

The authors' explanation is that AI conditions people to expect instant answers, so they lose practice working through difficulty. Their recommendation is that AI development should prioritize long-term competence as well as immediate task completion.

Limits: it is a preprint, and the sources I read describe short-term lab effects that do not establish lasting harm. I could not confirm per-experiment sample sizes, session lengths or the split between direct-answer and hint conditions from a page I opened, so I leave those out.
The question to watch is whether the effect persists over weeks and in real work or study, and whether tools that give hints rather than answers avoid it.

articles.headline: Who pays if the AI bubble pops? A B Nvidia guarantee backs an OpenAI campus in Ohio
articles.summary: The American Prospect says Nvidia's credit support for OpenAI's lease at an Ohio data-center campus could total up to $105 billion. The piece is opinion; the filing details it cites are the factual part.
impacts: A supplier guaranteeing its customer's rent concentrates risk in a few connected companies.
Who pays for about $4.2B of transmission upgrades is not settled in published documents.
If AI revenue disappoints, backstops like these are where losses could surface.
details: The American Prospect's Winton Woods, in a November 23 analysis, cites The Economist's estimate that AI model makers take in about $200 billion a year and would need about $3 trillion by 2030 to earn an ordinary return on infrastructure. The piece also says AI revenue growth fell from 80–90% per quarter last spring to 12% in October; it names no source for that figure in what I read.

The project is the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus near Piketon, Ohio, on the former Portsmouth uranium enrichment site. SB Energy and affiliates are the developers, and OpenAI has contracted the capacity under a long-term lease. AEP Ohio describes about $4.2 billion of associated transmission investment and says the developer, not existing customers, will pay. Rent starts only when power and readiness conditions are met.

The developer cites more than $6 billion in credit support, but its SEC filing says a termination payment could differ from the collateral posted and that project financing is generally nonrecourse. The filing also shows an accumulated deficit in the billions and project debt due within a few years.

Nvidia supplies the computing equipment, has invested in SB Energy and has provided credit support for OpenAI's lease obligations. Its latest quarterly report puts maximum exposure under those guarantees at up to $105 billion. OpenAI is also an SB Energy investor.

Ohio rules require 12-year contracts, payment for 85% of subscribed capacity, collateral and a termination charge of three years of minimum payments. A proposed 765 kV line would run about 51 miles from Pike County to Gallia County; the article says the agreement that would settle who bears the transmission cost has not been published, and a FERC study agreement has been filed.
The author's opinion, not fact, is that the structure resembles the 2007 mortgage market, where each party may assume someone else carries the risk. Treat that comparison as one commentator's view.

articles.headline: Treasury sold $766 billion of debt in one week as the 30-year hit 5.47% and CPI ran at 4.0%
articles.summary: Wolf Street's November 14 review says Treasury sold $766 billion in nine auctions as yields jumped on a hot inflation print. The data are from one blog's tally and the interpretation is opinion.
impacts: Higher yields raise the government's borrowing costs and mortgage and loan rates.
The article says markets price about two Fed rate hikes.
Weak auction demand can push yields up further.
details: Wolf Street, in a November 14 post using data as of Friday, November 13, reports that the 10-year Treasury yield was 5.15%, up 29 basis points on the week, with a low of 4.82% on November 5 and 5.31% at the October 5 high. The 20-year was 5.52%, the 30-year 5.47% (up 21 bp) and the 2-year 4.88% (up 37 bp), about 100 bp above the effective fed funds rate. The 6-month was 4.42%, the highest since December 2024.

Treasury sold $766 billion in nine auctions that week: $70 billion of 3-year notes at 4.627%, a 10-year at 5.020% (14 bp above its pre-CPI secondary-market level), $30 billion of 30-year bonds at 5.441%, and six T-bill auctions of about $616 billion. The page gives no auction tails, bid-to-cover or indirect-bidder data.

On inflation, the page says CPI is 4.0%, core CPI rose 0.30% month on month, and the PPI shows businesses facing 6.5% inflation, the worst since November 2022. It says Governor Waller's trigger for preferring a 50 bp hike at the December FOMC was reached by the core CPI print, and that the market prices about two hikes.

The author's views are opinion: the yield uptrend is 'intact', and the bond bear market is about six years old after the bull market that ended in August 2020. Reader comments predicting 6% on the 10-year or a 2027 recession are unverified and should be ignored as evidence.
Earlier days on this page covered the 5% yield milestone; the new part here is the auction week and the inflation inputs. Watch the December FOMC and the next auctions for whether demand holds.
